name: Feature map, runtime and state-machine proofs, and review with before/after captures
description: Use cases learn their surfaces and dependencies, drivers run the application through them, state machines are proved exhaustively when finite, action-sequence properties are evidenced, and reviewers see before/after captures, statecharts and verdicts per intent.
prose:
# Feature map, runtime and state-machine proofs, and review with before/after captures

Lastro learns how a user reaches each use case, runs the application through that path, proves state machines
exhaustively when they are finite, and shows the reviewer what changed on screen next to the intents and verdicts.
The engines stay the judges: Lastro never writes or fixes application code, and its only AI steps stay intent
extraction (with the survey that reads code) and proof derivation.

## The feature map

A use case may carry surfaces and dependencies. A surface says how a user reaches the use case from the user's
point of view: its kind (screen, route, command or api), a name in the user's words ("the left sidebar's chat list")
and a locator the driver understands (a URL path, a CLI command, a selector). A dependency names another use case
this one needs to work (opening a chat depends on signing in). The extraction step proposes surfaces and dependencies
for every use case an intent adds or modifies, and the reviewer approves them with the intent, like the description.
A use case with no surface is not reachable by the driver and is listed as such.

`lastro features` prints the feature map: every use case with its surfaces, what it depends on and what depends on
it. It is deterministic. It rejects a dependency on a use case that does not exist or that was removed, and a
dependency cycle, naming the use cases in it. When a proposal changes a use case, the map lists the use cases that
depend on it, directly or not, as affected: their proofs and captures run again with the proposal's own.

For a repository whose use cases have no surfaces yet, `lastro bootstrap --features` asks the survey step to read the
code and propose surfaces and dependencies for them. It writes a bootstrap proposal whose intents only add surfaces
and dependencies, never change a description, and that proposal is reviewed like any other.

## Driving the application

A driver is a process named in `.lastro/config.json` under `drivers`, written in any language, that Lastro starts
and talks to over JSON lines: Lastro sends a surface and a list of user actions (open, click, type, press, wait for),
and the driver answers with the observed state (named values the model declares as outputs) and the paths of the
captures it took. Lastro ships no browser of its own; the docs show a Playwright driver for web and Electron apps
and a process driver for CLIs.

A scenario may name a surface and a list of actions instead of a concrete input. It then runs through the driver:
the expectation is checked against the observed state, the result is empirical evidence, and a driver that fails to
start or times out fails the scenario with the driver's error, never passes it.

## State-machine proofs

A model may be a state machine: state variables with finite domains, an initial state, and events, each with finite
inputs. The code under proof is a step function from a state and an event to the next state. Clauses are of three
kinds: an invariant must hold in every reachable state; a step clause relates a state, an event and the next state;
a reachability clause says a state that satisfies a condition can be reached, which guards the other clauses against
proving nothing.

When the reachable state space has at most 100,000 states, Lastro visits all of it breadth first, and a clause that
holds everywhere it applies is proved, with formal evidence and the number of states visited. A larger or unbounded
space is explored by random walks from the initial state with a fixed seed, and a clause that holds is evidenced,
never proved. A violation comes back as the shortest sequence of events from the initial state that reaches it. The
TypeScript engine, the Rust prover, the Go SDK and the .NET SDK visit the states in the same order and give the same
verdicts and counterexamples.

## Properties over user action sequences

A property-based check names a surface, the actions a user can take there and an invariant over the observed state.
Lastro generates action sequences with a fixed seed, runs each through the driver and checks the invariant after
every action. A property that holds on every sequence is evidenced, with the number of sequences and actions run and
the rule-of-three failure bound; it is never proved. A failing sequence is shortened to the shortest prefix that
still fails and then replayed once: if the replay does not fail, the check is reported as nondeterministic instead of
violated.

## Before and after captures

When a proposal is extracted, every intent that touches a use case with a screen or route surface gets a before
capture: Lastro runs that surface's scenarios through the driver on the current code and stores what the driver
captured. When the proposal is proved, the same scenarios run on the new code and give the after capture. Captures
live in `.lastro/captures/<proposal>/<use case>/before|after/` and are never committed to git; the proposal records
the SHA-256 of each capture, so anyone can capture again and see whether the result still matches. A pixel
comparison of each before and after pair is computed deterministically and reported as the share of pixels changed.

An intent whose promise is a matter of human judgment (the layout looks right, the message is clear) stays beyond
proof, but after the proof run it waits for a sign-off: a reviewer looks at its before and after captures and signs
it off or requests changes. A proposal is not proved while such an intent waits for its sign-off.

## Reviewing the evidence

The review app shows, for each intent: the use case's place in the feature map (its surfaces, what it depends on and
what it affects), the statechart drawn from its state-machine model when it has one, its before capture during the
review and its before and after captures with the pixel comparison after the proof run, and the verdict of every
proof and property with its counterexample. The receipt adds a Feature map section with the affected use cases, a
state diagram in Mermaid for every state-machine model, the captures with their hashes and pixel comparison, and the
sign-offs with who gave them.

The CLI, the TypeScript, Go and .NET SDKs, the docs and the plugin's skills cover all of this, and the plugin's
review shows the captures' paths and the sign-offs still due.

useCases.name: Store use cases and proposals
useCases.before: The workspace keeps one file per entity: each use case in .lastro/usecases/<id>-<slug>.json (id, slug, name, description, history), each proof of a use case in .lastro/proof/<proof-id>-<slug>.json and each proposal in .lastro/proposals/<id>-<slug>.json, with its receipt next to it. Use cases are numbered UC-001, UC-002... and proposals P-001, P-002... with the next free number, never reused even after a removal; intents and proofs are numbered inside their proposal (P-007.I-03, P-007.PF-05) and keep that id when a proof moves to its use case; proofs derived straight from a use case are numbered inside it (UC-003.PF-01). Slugs are kebab-case and stable: a rename changes only the name. intents.json, spec.json and proof.json are no longer written. A use case file that still carries a proofs list is read as before, and its proofs move to .lastro/proof/ the next time the workspace writes that use case.

useCases.name: Extract intents from prose
useCases.before: propose(prose, { submittedBy }) creates the next proposal file in .lastro/proposals/ with status open and sends the prose and the current use cases to an LLM through an AskJson transport with a fixed system prompt and JSON Schema (step "extract"). The answer lists intents, each the addition, removal or change of exactly one use case: id (P-n.I-nn), slug, name, a natural-language description of the change, change (add, modify or remove), the use case (an existing id, or a newly reserved id and slug for an add), a provability (formal, empirical, beyond-proof), a beyondProofReason ("none" or one of the five reasons) and a verbatim quote, and replaces: the existing proofs of that use case the new behavior contradicts, each with a reason (extraction receives every touched use case with its proofs in readable notation; for a remove the SDK lists every proof of the use case itself); one resulting use case per touched use case with its name and, for add and modify, the complete new description (after), all its intents combined, and the intents that produce it; decisions that reference intents by zero-based index; and notPromised items. The SDK fills each modify and remove with the use case's current description (before); the LLM never supplies it. The proposal (lastro: proposal/v1) records the baseline (sha256 over the canonical use cases without their proofs), the submitter, every intent proposed with no approvals, decisions D1, D2... with origin extraction, and the review policy. Intents have no kind. Without an LLM transport or a custom extractor, propose() throws.
useCases.after: propose(prose, { submittedBy }) creates the next proposal file in .lastro/proposals/ with status open and sends the prose and the current use cases to an LLM through an AskJson transport with a fixed system prompt and JSON Schema (step "extract"). For every use case it adds or modifies, the answer also proposes surfaces and dependencies, stored with the after and reviewed with its intents. The SDK fills each modify and remove with the use case's current description (before); the LLM never supplies it. The proposal (lastro: proposal/v1) records the baseline (sha256 over the canonical use cases without their proofs), the submitter, every intent proposed with no approvals, decisions D1, D2... with origin extraction, and the review policy. Intents have no kind. Without an LLM transport or a custom extractor, propose() throws.

It calls coverage complete when every input of the space has a row and no row is nondeterministic or out of domain; an input repeated with the same output still counts as covered once. It says proved only with complete coverage, checks vacuity, mutants and consistency itself, and returns a SHA-256 digest of the table. The proof is ok only if the SDK report is ok, the prover is ok and both engines give every clause the same verdict.

useCases.name: Render a receipt
useCases.before: The receipt is Markdown for a pull request, written next to the proposal: the overall result and counts per verdict; the proposal and plan hashes; the Rust check with coverage, table digest and whether verdicts agree; the use-case diff, with each use case added, modified (before and after) or removed with the intents behind it, each replaced proof next to the proofs that take its place, each superseded proof that still passes, each regression and, after apply, the new baseline hash; a table of intents with verdict, evidence, confidence and what backs each; notes; each proof with verdict, evidence, method (exhaustive, samples with failure bound, traces), mutants killed, formal statement, counterexample, violating trace and notes; trusted pieces; where proof stops; not promised; and pending contradictions.
useCases.after: The receipt is Markdown for a pull request, written next to the proposal: the overall result and counts per verdict; the proposal and plan hashes; the Rust check with coverage, table digest and whether verdicts agree; the use-case diff, with each use case added, modified (before and after) or removed with the intents behind it, each replaced proof next to the proofs that take its place, each superseded proof that still passes, each regression and, after apply, the new baseline hash; a table of intents with verdict, evidence, confidence and what backs each; notes; each proof with verdict, evidence, method (exhaustive, samples with failure bound, traces), mutants killed, formal statement, counterexample, violating trace and notes; trusted pieces; where proof stops; not promised; pending contradictions; a Feature map section with the affected use cases; a Mermaid state diagram for every state-machine model; the captures with their hashes and pixel comparison; and the sign-offs with who gave them.

useCases.name: Use Lastro from TypeScript, .NET or Go
useCases.before: Three SDKs expose the same pipeline (propose against the use cases, review with threads, pending, derive, returnDecisions, prove with the regression run, apply, gap review) with the same entities (use case, proposal, intent, proof), wire format, canonical hashes, seeded sampling, verdicts, receipts and prompts. Cross-check tests compare the .NET and Go reports and hashes with the TypeScript SDK, and all three with the Rust prover, on the reference login and its planted bugs.
useCases.after: Three SDKs expose the same pipeline (propose against the use cases, review with threads, pending, derive, returnDecisions, prove with the regression run, apply, gap review) with the same entities (use case, proposal, intent, proof), wire format, canonical hashes, seeded sampling, verdicts, receipts and prompts. Cross-check tests compare the .NET and Go reports and hashes with the TypeScript SDK, and all three with the Rust prover, on the reference login and its planted bugs. Surfaces, the feature map, drivers, state-machine proofs, action-sequence properties, captures and sign-offs are in all three SDKs and the CLI, with the same files, hashes and verdicts, and the docs describe them.

useCases.name: Review an agent's proposal like a pull request
useCases.before: The plugin's propose skill has the agent write the change as prose in .lastro/proposals/<id>-<slug>.md, run lastro propose (answering handoffs itself), show the user the review the plugin renders as Markdown (the PostToolUse hook adds it to the agent's context after the first lastro command that shows a new or re-extracted proposal in a session, and a one-line summary after later ones; lastro-plugin.mjs review prints it), then ask the user every open decision and, per intent, shown with the existing proofs it replaces, approve, request changes (amend) or reject, recording only the user's answers with lastro review --as <user>, until lastro status is ready; then lastro derive writes the proposal's proofs. The PreToolUse hook makes every lastro review command that approves, answers, amends or rejects show a Claude Code permission prompt, and denies it in both harnesses when --as names an agent (claude, codex, agent, assistant, ai, bot). With a policy above one approval the board shows each intent's approvals out of the required number and the proposal waits for the other reviewers.
useCases.after: The plugin's propose skill has the agent write the change as prose in .lastro/proposals/<id>-<slug>.md, run lastro propose (answering handoffs itself), show the user the review the plugin renders as Markdown (the PostToolUse hook adds it to the agent's context after the first lastro command that shows a new or re-extracted proposal in a session, and a one-line summary after later ones; lastro-plugin.mjs review prints it), then ask the user every open decision and, per intent, shown with the existing proofs it replaces, approve, request changes (amend) or reject, recording only the user's answers with lastro review --as <user>, until lastro status is ready; then lastro derive writes the proposal's proofs. The PreToolUse hook makes every lastro review command that approves, answers, amends or rejects show a Claude Code permission prompt, and denies it in both harnesses when --as names an agent (claude, codex, agent, assistant, ai, bot). With a policy above one approval the board shows each intent's approvals out of the required number and the proposal waits for the other reviewers. The review also lists the captures' paths and the sign-offs still due.

decisions.name: Driver timeout
decisions.question: What is the driver timeout that fails a driven scenario?

options.label: 30 s per action, configurable
options.consequence: drivers.<name>.timeoutMs in config.json, default 30000 per action.

options.label: One limit per scenario
options.consequence: Long flows need one large number; a single slow action is harder to locate.

decisions.name: How many sign-offs
decisions.question: How many reviewers must sign off a human-judgment intent after the proof run?

options.label: The review policy's approvals
options.consequence: Same quorum as approving intents (review.approvals in config.json).

options.label: Always one
options.consequence: Faster, but a single reviewer can accept a visual change a policy of two would not.

decisions.name: Where captures live
decisions.question: Captures stay out of git, so a reviewer on another machine sees them only after capturing again. Is that acceptable?

options.label: Out of git, hashes only
options.consequence: Matches the rule of never committing screenshots; other reviewers re-run the driver to see them.

options.label: Upload to the review app's storage
options.consequence: Reviewers anywhere see them, but Lastro needs a storage backend and stops being file-only.

options.label: Commit with Git LFS
options.consequence: Everyone sees them in the PR, but it breaks the no-screenshots-in-git rule.

notPromised: Lastro does not ship a browser or a Playwright dependency in the SDKs.
TLA+ and Lean specifications are not read or run by Lastro.
A pixel change does not fail a proof by itself; it is only reported.
Captures are not compared across machines or operating systems for equality.
Lastro does not generate the driver for an application.
